title: Lists
objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to store several values in a list, read and add items, and loop over them.

sections.title: What is a list?
sections.text: A list holds many values in one variable, in order. You write it with square brackets and commas: fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"].

sections.title: Indexes start at 0
sections.text: Each item has a position number called an index. The first item is at index 0. fruits[0] is "apple" and fruits[2] is "cherry". Asking for an index that is too big causes an IndexError.

sections.title: Adding and changing items
sections.text: fruits.append("mango") adds an item to the end. fruits[1] = "grape" replaces the item at index 1. len(fruits) tells you how many items the list has.

sections.title: Lists and loops
sections.text: You can loop over a list: for f in fruits: print(f). The loop body runs once for every item, so you never have to count the items yourself.

check_questions.explanation: Index 1 is the second item, so it prints green.

misconception.0: Index 0 is red. Index 1 is the second item.
misconception.3: 1 is the index, not the item.

check_questions.prompt: How many items are in the list after this code runs?
check_questions.explanation: The list starts with 2 items and append adds a third, so len(nums) is 3.

misconception.0: append adds an item, so the list grows.
misconception.2: 7 is the value added, not the number of items.
misconception.3: len counts items. It does not add the values.
